clinkered material is often of good quality because its source is usually from recent rainfall and snowmelt. The clinkered material is normally fractured and the fracture system results in a relatively high permeability. The concentration of the dissolved solids of this water is low, and includes ions of magnesium, calcium, and sulfate (Hopkins, 1973). This water is termed "hard water", in reference to its soap consumption. Locally, most groundwater from clinker contains magnesium sulfate (epsom salt) at concentrations which may make it unsatisfactory for human consumption but acceptable for household use.
Water from the slope wash and alluvium deposits also contains magnesium, calcium and sulfate and is termed "hard". Dissolved solids concentrations of this water are usually higher than water from the clinker deposits. Some slope wash springs contain excessive magnesium sulfate.
Chemical composition of ground water in sandstone and coal bed aquifers in the Tongue River Member depends primarily on the depth at which the aquifer is tapped since the quality varies according to the characteristics of the aquifer. The sandy beds of the Lebo Shale member contain water too highly mineralized to be used for domestic or livestock supplies (U.S. Department of the Interior, 1974).
U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs (1974), cites data from two sources:

1) notes on the quality of ground water in the aquifers of the Sarpy

Creek and Tullock Creek drainage basins; and 2) selected chemical

analyses of wells and springs on Westmoreland Resources Tract III.

These data are from analyses of water samples collected by the Montana

Bureau of Mines and Geology.
